title: From setup to a stock chart in nine notebooks

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture a beginner on day one of learning Python. By the end of the workshop, they're plotting Apple's stock price with five moving average curves. How do you get someone from zero to that?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's a big jump. I'd guess most beginner courses lose people somewhere around installing things.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Antoine's AlgoETS Workshop1 is built to avoid exactly that. It's a GitHub repository with nine Jupyter notebooks, spread over six numbered folders. Each folder gives the next concept somewhere to go.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So it's like a staircase rather than a pile of lessons.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. First comes setup, then Python basics and more advanced Python, then reading an API response, then cleaning and exploring data with pandas, then two notebooks on visualization, and finally a project that ties it all together.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What about the setup part? That's usually where people give up.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The README offers a Colab link, so you can start writing code in your browser right away. Running Jupyter locally is documented too. So setup is its own topic, but it never blocks the first lesson.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Nice. And the final project is the Apple stock one?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. The last notebook asks for Apple price data, then plots the closing price along with exponential moving averages over 12, 26, 50, 100 and 200 days. Think of an EMA as a smoothed line that follows the price, with the shorter ones hugging it and the longer ones drifting behind.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So you use everything you learned. A request, a table, new columns, and a labeled chart.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right, and that's why it works as teaching. You can ask real technical questions of the chart. Are the dates in order? Why does a longer average react more slowly? Are all the curves computed from the same observations?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Those are great classroom questions. And the numbered folders mean you can go back to one idea without redoing the whole thing.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. If pandas feels shaky, you jump back to that folder and come forward again.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Does it lead anywhere after the chart?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Antoine describes a natural next step, his BatchBacktesting project. Same indicator idea, but run across many instruments with the assumptions recorded, so results are comparable.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So understand one chart first, then scale it up.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the takeaway. Give each concept a place to land, and a beginner ends up reading real data and real code. The full write-up has the flow diagram and links to every notebook.
